Action Plan:
1. Patient to arrange comprehensive blood tests via the support line: complete blood count, renal & liver function, thyroid profile, Lyme serology, and other fatigue-screening tests as per local panel (e.g., viral serology, iron studies, vitamin D) – to be done as soon as possible.
2. Follow-up telephone consultation to be scheduled ~1 week after bloods are taken to review results and ongoing symptoms.
3. If Lyme serology returns positive, commence standard first-line oral antibiotics for early Lyme disease (drug/dose/duration per local guideline – not yet prescribed).
4. Advise patient to seek earlier review if worsening fatigue, new neurological/cardiac symptoms, joint swelling, or recurrent rash develops.
5. Reinforce regular use of preventive asthma inhaler; encourage continuation of current OTC antihistamine for hay-fever control.
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: 6-week history of feeling “tired, run-down” with diffuse aching (shoulders, back, hips, knees).  
• Timeline: Well at Christmas/New Year; onset ∼mid-February (~2 weeks after returning from holiday in the United States).  
• Rash: Single, non-itchy annular lesion on back of left calf first noticed mid-/late February; faded over 1-2 weeks; photo shown during consult. Mild sore throat and possible low-grade fever at that time.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild headaches; reduced appetite (no weight change). Denies respiratory, GI, GU, neurologic symptoms; no joint swelling.  
• Functional impact: Continuing to work but with reduced energy/concentration; decreased exercise. Mental health currently good.  
• Past medical history: Asthma, hay fever.  
• Medications: Preventive inhaler (name/dose/route/frequency not documented; taken morning & night); OTC antihistamine (name/dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Social: Lives with wife; works in health-technology; occasional alcohol; smoking status not clearly stated. Enjoys hiking/walking (wore shorts while in U.S.).  
• Allergies: Not documented.

Objective:
(No in-consult examination performed; no vitals recorded.)

Assessment & Plan:

1. Fatigue with generalized myalgia  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Suspected Lyme disease (early disseminated). Supported by DDx “Lyme disease – High likelihood.”  
   – Differential diagnosis:  
     • Post-viral or chronic viral infection (DDx: Medium).  
     • Hypothyroidism (DDx: Medium).  
     • Iron-deficiency or other anemia (DDx: Low).  
     • Early autoimmune/connective-tissue disease such as SLE or inflammatory arthritis (DDx: Low).  
   – Investigations planned: CBC; urea, electrolytes & creatinine; liver function tests; thyroid profile (TSH ± FT4); Lyme IgM/IgG serology; consider EBV/CMV serology, ferritin, vitamin D as per fatigue screen.  
   – Treatment planned: If Lyme positive, commence guideline-recommended oral antibiotic course (e.g., doxycycline – dose/duration per protocol). Symptomatic advice; monitor.  
   – Relevant referrals: None at present; rheumatology or infectious diseases if atypical results or persistent symptoms.

2. Resolved calf rash  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Erythema migrans secondary to Lyme disease.  
   – Differential diagnosis: Hypersensitivity vasculitis, viral exanthem (less likely).  
   – Investigations planned: Addressed via Lyme serology above (no biopsy indicated).  
   – Treatment planned: As per Issue 1 if Lyme confirmed.  
   – Relevant referrals: Dermatology only if recurrence or diagnostic uncertainty.

3. Asthma (stable)  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Stable asthma; no recent exacerbations.  
   – Differential diagnosis: N/A.  
   – Investigations planned: None.  
   – Treatment planned: Continue preventive inhaler regularly; reinforce adherence.  
   – Relevant referrals: None.

Quality checks:
• Missing documentation: Allergy status, smoking status, exact medication names/doses, vitals, systems review of sleep pattern and mood screen.  
• Internal conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Generally clear; brief audio dropout near end but did not affect clinical content.
